notes.front: In EBM, what is an input?
notes.back: One of five categories of measures: things the organisation spends money on.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the five categories of measures the EBM Guide lists.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience.
notes.example: Like a team’s cloud-hosting bill or its training budget: money spent that makes delivery possible, but says nothing yet about what customers gain.

notes.front: In EBM, what is an activity?
notes.back: One of five categories of measures: things people in the organisation do, such as going to meetings or writing code.
notes.explanation: Activities sit alongside inputs, outputs, outcomes and impacts in the guide’s five categories of measures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Activities. These are things that people in the organization do, such as perform work, go to meetings, have discussions, write code, create reports, attend conferences, and so forth.
notes.example: Like the hours a team logs on a timesheet: a record of effort, which is different from the features it produces or what customers gain.

notes.front: What does EBM add to the organisational improvement process?
notes.back: It makes the forming of hypotheses, measuring of results and adapting of goals explicit and transparent.
notes.explanation: That work is already an implicit part of an agile approach; EBM’s contribution is to make it explicit and transparent.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Explicitly forming hypotheses, measuring results, and inspecting and adapting goals based on those results are implicit parts of an agile approach. Making this work explicit and transparent is what EBM adds to the organizational improvement process.

notes.front: Which impediment to A2I in the EBM Guide’s list concerns time lost to quality problems?
notes.back: Spending too much time remedying poor product quality.
notes.explanation: The guide’s list is open (“and so on”); this is one example among others.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality

notes.front: In the EBM Guide’s list of A2I impediments, what lack forces an organisation to maintain multiple variations of a product?
notes.explanation: The guide gives it as one example of what can impede an organisation from delivering new capabilities and value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality, needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence

notes.front: Which kind of decision-making does the EBM Guide name as lacking, in its list of A2I impediments?
notes.explanation: It appears in an open list of things that can impede delivering new capabilities and value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: lack of operational excellence, lack of decentralized decision-making, inability to hire

notes.front: Which people-related impediment to A2I does the EBM Guide name?
notes.back: An inability to hire and inspire talented, passionate team members.
notes.explanation: It is the last named item in an open list that ends “and so on”.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality, needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence, lack of decentralized decision-making, inability to hire and inspire talented, passionate

notes.front: Besides internal impediments, what else reduces A2I, according to the EBM Guide?
notes.back: Anything that stops users or customers benefiting from innovation, such as products or new versions that are hard to assemble or install.
notes.explanation: The guide adds this to the internal impediments as something that will also reduce A2I.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: benefiting from innovation, such as hard to assemble/install products or new versions of products, will also reduce A2I.

notes.front: In EBM, what is the next step after achieving an Immediate Tactical Goal?
notes.back: Form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that will take you closer to your Intermediate Goal.
notes.explanation: You keep devising experiments toward the new goal, step by step.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Your next step will be to form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that, when achieved, will take you closer to your Intermediate Goal. Continue devising experiments, or things you can try, to achieve that goal.

notes.front: At which level of goals may EBM goals need adjusting, or turn out to be no longer relevant?
notes.explanation: A goal may prove no longer relevant or need refining, whether it is strategic, intermediate or immediate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Sometimes you’ll find that your goals need adjusting. You might discover that a goal is no longer relevant, or that it needs to be refined. This can happen to your goals at any level.

notes.front: A director says: “We doubled this product’s budget and headcount, so customers must be getting twice the value.” As Scrum Master, what does EBM suggest you point out?
notes.back: B) There is no correlation between the amount of input and the value customers experience, so look at customer outcomes
notes.explanation: Budget and headcount are inputs, and the EBM Guide says their amount does not correlate with customer value.
notes.choices:
A) The claim holds, because inputs are necessary to produce value
B) There is no correlation between the amount of input and the value customers experience, so look at customer outcomes
C) Value should be proven by counting the hours the teams now log
D) Value should be proven by counting the features shipped since the increase
notes.choicesExplained: A mistakes “necessary” for “proportional”. C and D swap one easy measure (activities, outputs) for another; neither shows what customers experience.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience.

notes.front: A team’s dashboard shows hours logged, items completed and features shipped, all rising. A stakeholder asks whether customers are actually better off. What should the Scrum Master help the team add?
notes.back: C) Measures of customer outcomes, even though they are harder to gather
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says activities and outputs are easy to measure but outcomes are difficult, and that more work and features do not necessarily improve customer experience.
notes.choices:
A) More output measures, such as releases per month
B) More precise tracking of hours per item
C) Measures of customer outcomes, even though they are harder to gather
D) Nothing: rising outputs show that value is rising
notes.choicesExplained: A and B add more of the easy measures the dashboard already has. D contradicts the guide: more hours and features do not necessarily improve customer experience.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Organizations may gather a lot of data with insufficient information about their ability to deliver value. However, delivering valuable outcomes to customers is essential if organizations are to reach their goals. For example, working more hours (activities) and delivering more features (outputs) does not necessarily lead to improved customer experiences (outcomes).

notes.front: To hit a quarterly profit target, management proposes cutting testing and shipping lower-quality updates. The Scrum Master is asked what the EBM Guide says about improving impacts this way. What is the answer?
notes.back: A) It is possible, but improving impacts without improving customer outcomes usually harms the organisation
notes.explanation: The guide gives reducing product quality to improve profitability as an example of harmful impact-chasing.
notes.choices:
A) It is possible, but improving impacts without improving customer outcomes usually harms the organisation
B) It cannot raise profit at all
C) It is fine, because profit is an impact and impacts are what matter
D) It is acceptable as long as it lasts only one quarter
notes.choicesExplained: C ignores the guide’s warning about harm. B overstates: the guide says it is possible. D adds a time limit the guide never gives.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While it is possible for organizations to improve impacts without improving customer outcomes, doing so usually harms the organization, such as when it reduces product quality to improve profitability

notes.front: A Product Owner picks features because “we just know users want them”. Nobody states what each feature should achieve, and nobody checks afterwards. How can the Scrum Master use EBM to help?
notes.back: D) Help the Product Owner make each feature’s hypothesis about value explicit, with a measure to check it
notes.explanation: EBM treats features as hypotheses about value and makes testing them explicit and transparent.
notes.choices:
A) Leave it: good Product Owners rely on instinct
B) Ask stakeholders to vote on each feature instead
C) Stop building features until market research is complete
D) Help the Product Owner make each feature’s hypothesis about value explicit, with a measure to check it
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the beliefs untested. B swaps one untested belief for another. C halts delivery instead of learning through experiments.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Every feature and every requirement really represents a hypothesis about value. One of the goals of an empirical approach is to make these hypotheses explicit and to consciously design experiments that explicitly test the value of the features and requirements.

notes.front: A team plans to spend three Sprints building a complete recommendation engine before any user sees it. The riskiest assumption is whether users will use recommendations at all. What could the Scrum Master suggest?
notes.back: C) Build just enough to validate that critical assumption first
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says building enough of a feature to validate critical assumptions may be sufficient to judge its value.
notes.choices:
A) Skip testing the assumption and rely on stakeholder opinion
B) Build the full engine, since a partial one proves nothing
C) Build just enough to validate that critical assumption first
D) Wait until the whole Product Backlog is refined before starting
notes.choicesExplained: B contradicts the guide: the whole feature need not be built to judge its value. A relies on opinion, and the guide says beliefs about value stay assumptions until customers validate them. D delays learning without testing anything.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: A team spends a third of every Sprint merging fixes into four separately maintained versions of its product, one per client. Which A2I impediment named in the EBM Guide does this match?
notes.back: D) Maintaining multiple variations of a product due to a lack of operational excellence
notes.explanation: Keeping several variations of one product alive is the guide’s own example of this impediment.
notes.choices:
A) A lack of decentralised decision-making
B) Too much time spent on stakeholder meetings
C) An inability to hire and inspire talented team members
D) Maintaining multiple variations of a product due to a lack of operational excellence
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are other items on the list but do not describe keeping several versions alive. B is not one of the guide’s named examples.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality, needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence, lack of decentralized decision-making, inability to hire and inspire talented, passionate

notes.front: A Scrum Master is helping a team choose its next Immediate Tactical Goal. Every option is internal: faster builds, fewer merge conflicts, shorter meetings. None mentions customers. What should the Scrum Master raise?
notes.back: B) Goals aimed only at A2I and T2M, without watching CV and UV, may not help customers
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide warns that improving only A2I and T2M without monitoring CV and UV focuses on internal processes, and can signal a lack of outcome-based goals.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: any measurable goal will do
B) Goals aimed only at A2I and T2M, without watching CV and UV, may not help customers
C) Internal goals are not allowed in EBM
D) Add a budget target, since inputs drive value
notes.choicesExplained: A misses the guide’s warning that internal-only goals may not help customers. C overstates: the guide allows such goals but says to keep CV and UV in view. D treats inputs as value, which the guide says do not correlate with it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: When an organization targets improvements only in A2I and T2M without monitoring CV and UV, they are focused only on internal processes that may not help them further satisfy customers or achieve value. This can lead to, or be an indication of, a lack of outcome-based goals.

notes.front: A team’s experiment to raise sign-ups with a shorter form did not work, and a manager calls it “a wasted Sprint”. How should the Scrum Master frame it, using EBM?
notes.back: B) Missing an Immediate Tactical Goal because an experiment failed is not a bad thing; the learning shapes new experiments
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says such a failure is not bad, because what you learn helps devise better experiments.
notes.choices:
A) Agree, and ask the team to avoid experiments whose results are uncertain
B) Missing an Immediate Tactical Goal because an experiment failed is not a bad thing; the learning shapes new experiments
C) Report it as a failure of the Product Owner
D) Repeat the same experiment until it succeeds
notes.choicesExplained: A would stop the experimenting EBM relies on. C looks for blame instead of learning. D ignores what the result has taught.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: And sometimes you’ll fail to reach your Immediate Tactical Goal because your experiment did not produce the results you had expected. This is not a bad thing, and what you learned helps you to devise new experiments that may yield better results.

notes.front: Halfway to an Intermediate Goal, a change in regulation makes the goal irrelevant. The team wants to carry on “because we committed to it”. What does EBM suggest?
notes.back: C) Adjust or replace the goal: goals at any level may need adjusting or stop being relevant
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide expects goals to need adjusting, at any level, as you learn.
notes.choices:
A) Carry on, because EBM goals are fixed once set
B) Keep the goal but stop measuring progress
C) Adjust or replace the goal: goals at any level may need adjusting or stop being relevant
D) Drop EBM for this product
notes.choicesExplained: A contradicts the guide. B removes the evidence EBM depends on. D abandons the approach instead of adapting the goal.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Sometimes you’ll find that your goals need adjusting. You might discover that a goal is no longer relevant, or that it needs to be refined. This can happen to your goals at any level.
